prompt: A force of 150 N is applied at right angles to a spanner 150 mm from the centre of a nut. Find the moment (torque) on the nut.
why: M = F × d = 150 × 0.15 m = 22.5 N m; convert mm to m first.

prompt: A force of 250 N is applied at right angles to a spanner 350 mm from the centre of a nut. Find the moment (torque) on the nut.
why: M = F × d = 250 × 0.35 m = 87.5 N m; convert mm to m first.

prompt: A force of 120 N is applied at right angles to a spanner 600 mm from the centre of a nut. Find the moment (torque) on the nut.
why: M = F × d = 120 × 0.6 m = 72.0 N m; convert mm to m first.

prompt: A uniform beam pivots at its centre. A 200 N load sits 0.5 m to the left of the pivot. What downward force must act 2.4 m to the right of the pivot to balance it?
why: Taking moments about the pivot: 200 × 0.5 = F × 2.4, so F = 41.7 N.

prompt: A uniform beam pivots at its centre. A 450 N load sits 0.8 m to the left of the pivot. What downward force must act 1.6 m to the right of the pivot to balance it?
why: Taking moments about the pivot: 450 × 0.8 = F × 1.6, so F = 225 N.

prompt: A uniform beam pivots at its centre. A 200 N load sits 0.8 m to the left of the pivot. What downward force must act 2.5 m to the right of the pivot to balance it?
why: Taking moments about the pivot: 200 × 0.8 = F × 2.5, so F = 64.0 N.

prompt: A uniform beam pivots at its centre. An 800 N load sits 0.5 m to the left of the pivot. What downward force must act 2.5 m to the right of the pivot to balance it?
why: Taking moments about the pivot: 800 × 0.5 = F × 2.5, so F = 160 N.

prompt: A 4 m beam is simply supported at both ends. A 9 kN point load acts 1 m from the left support. Find the reaction at the right support.
why: Take moments about the other support: R_right = 9 × 1/4 = 2.25 kN and R_left = 9 − 2.25 = 6.75 kN.

prompt: A 4 m beam is simply supported at both ends. A 12 kN point load acts 1 m from the left support. Find the reaction at the left support.
why: Take moments about the other support: R_right = 12 × 1/4 = 3.00 kN and R_left = 12 − 3.00 = 9.00 kN.

prompt: A 6 m beam is simply supported at both ends. A 6 kN point load acts 1 m from the left support. Find the reaction at the right support.
why: Take moments about the other support: R_right = 6 × 1/6 = 1.00 kN and R_left = 6 − 1.00 = 5.00 kN.

prompt: An 8 m beam is simply supported at both ends. A 6 kN point load acts 2 m from the left support. Find the reaction at the right support.
why: Take moments about the other support: R_right = 6 × 2/8 = 1.50 kN and R_left = 6 − 1.50 = 4.50 kN.

prompt: Two forces of 100 N and 60 N act away from the same point with an angle of 50° between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
why: Completing the parallelogram, R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cos θ, giving R = 146 N. (Using −2F₁F₂cos θ treats θ as the triangle angle instead.)

prompt: Two forces of 30 N and 80 N act away from the same point with an angle of 130° between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
why: Completing the parallelogram, R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cos θ, giving R = 64.9 N. (Using −2F₁F₂cos θ treats θ as the triangle angle instead.)

prompt: Two forces of 60 N and 80 N act away from the same point with an angle of 120° between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
why: Completing the parallelogram, R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cos θ, giving R = 72.1 N. (Using −2F₁F₂cos θ treats θ as the triangle angle instead.)

prompt: A 50 kg sign hangs from two identical cables, each at 60° to the horizontal and symmetric about the sign. Find the tension in each cable (g = 9.8 m/s²).
why: Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 60° = 490 N, so T = 283 N.

prompt: An 80 kg sign hangs from two identical cables, each at 20° to the horizontal and symmetric about the sign. Find the tension in each cable (g = 9.8 m/s²).
why: Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 20° = 784 N, so T = 1150 N.

prompt: A 120 kg sign hangs from two identical cables, each at 20° to the horizontal and symmetric about the sign. Find the tension in each cable (g = 9.8 m/s²).
why: Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 20° = 1180 N, so T = 1720 N.

prompt: For a rigid body acted on by coplanar forces to be in equilibrium,
options: the forces must all be parallel
ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point
why: No net force in either direction and no net moment, otherwise the body would accelerate or rotate.

prompt: The equilibrant of a system of forces is
options: the largest single force in the system
equal in size to the resultant but acts in the opposite direction
why: Adding the equilibrant cancels the resultant, giving equilibrium.

prompt: The principle of transmissibility states that a force
options: must act at the centre of mass
can be moved anywhere along its line of action without changing its effect on a rigid body
can be moved to any point on the body
loses size as it is moved
why: Only the line of action matters for a rigid body.

prompt: A couple is
options: two equal, opposite, parallel forces that are not collinear, producing pure rotation
a single force through the centre of mass
two forces acting in the same direction
why: A couple has zero resultant force but a moment equal to F × perpendicular distance between them.

prompt: The three-force rule states that if a body is in equilibrium under three non-parallel forces, the forces
options: must be concurrent, meeting at a single point
why: If the lines of action did not meet, there would be a net moment.

prompt: A free body diagram should show
options: the isolated body and all external forces acting on it
the internal forces in every part
why: Isolating the body and showing every external force allows equilibrium equations to be written.

prompt: A machine lifts a 2400 N load with an effort of 500 N. What is its mechanical advantage?
why: MA = load/effort = 2400/500 = 4.80.

prompt: A machine lifts a 1200 N load with an effort of 200 N. What is its mechanical advantage?
why: MA = load/effort = 1200/200 = 6.00.

prompt: A pulley system with a velocity ratio of 6 lifts a 1500 N load using an effort of 500 N. Find its efficiency.
A pulley system with a velocity ratio of 5 lifts an 800 N load using an effort of 300 N. Find its efficiency.
A pulley system with a velocity ratio of 5 lifts a 1200 N load using an effort of 450 N. Find its efficiency.
A driver gear with 12 teeth turns at 1200 rpm and meshes with a driven gear of 18 teeth. Find the speed of the driven gear.
why: N₂ = N₁ × T₁/T₂ = 1200 × 12/18 = 800 rpm. A smaller driven gear turns faster.

prompt: A driver gear with 24 teeth turns at 900 rpm and meshes with a driven gear of 40 teeth. Find the speed of the driven gear.
why: N₂ = N₁ × T₁/T₂ = 900 × 24/40 = 540 rpm. A smaller driven gear turns faster.

prompt: A driver gear with 30 teeth turns at 2400 rpm and meshes with a driven gear of 40 teeth. Find the speed of the driven gear.
why: N₂ = N₁ × T₁/T₂ = 2400 × 30/40 = 1800 rpm. A smaller driven gear turns faster.

prompt: A driver gear with 24 teeth turns at 1200 rpm and meshes with a driven gear of 48 teeth. Find the speed of the driven gear.
why: N₂ = N₁ × T₁/T₂ = 1200 × 24/48 = 600 rpm. A smaller driven gear turns faster.

prompt: In a compound gear train, gear A (12 teeth) drives gear B (45 teeth). Gear C (18 teeth) is fixed on the same shaft as B and drives gear D (40 teeth). Find the velocity ratio of the train (input A to output D).
why: VR = (driven/driver) × (driven/driver) = (45/12) × (40/18) = 8.33.

prompt: In a compound gear train, gear A (20 teeth) drives gear B (60 teeth). Gear C (10 teeth) is fixed on the same shaft as B and drives gear D (45 teeth). Find the velocity ratio of the train (input A to output D).
why: VR = (driven/driver) × (driven/driver) = (60/20) × (45/10) = 13.5.

prompt: In a compound gear train, gear A (12 teeth) drives gear B (36 teeth). Gear C (10 teeth) is fixed on the same shaft as B and drives gear D (40 teeth). Find the velocity ratio of the train (input A to output D).
why: VR = (driven/driver) × (driven/driver) = (36/12) × (40/10) = 12.0.

prompt: A block and tackle has 3 rope segments supporting the load block. Ignoring friction, what effort is needed to lift a 1200 N load?
why: With 3 supporting ropes, VR = 3; ideally MA = VR, so effort = 1200/3 = 400 N.

prompt: A block and tackle has 5 rope segments supporting the load block. Ignoring friction, what effort is needed to lift a 1800 N load?
why: With 5 supporting ropes, VR = 5; ideally MA = VR, so effort = 1800/5 = 360 N.

prompt: A screw jack has a handle that sweeps a circle of diameter 300 mm, and the screw has a pitch of 6 mm. What is its velocity ratio?
why: In one turn the effort moves πD = 942 mm and the load rises one pitch (6 mm), so VR = 157.

prompt: A screw jack has a handle that sweeps a circle of diameter 500 mm, and the screw has a pitch of 6 mm. What is its velocity ratio?
why: In one turn the effort moves πD = 1570 mm and the load rises one pitch (6 mm), so VR = 262.

prompt: A wheelbarrow is an example of which class of lever?
options: Class 1: the fulcrum is between load and effort
Class 2: the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
Class 3: the effort is between fulcrum and load
why: The wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the tray and the effort is at the handles.

prompt: Tweezers and the human forearm lifting a weight are class 3 levers. A class 3 lever always has
options: a mechanical advantage less than 1, but gains distance and speed
the fulcrum between load and effort
why: The effort is closer to the fulcrum than the load, so more force is needed but the load moves further.

prompt: An idler gear placed between a driver and a driven gear
options: reverses the direction of the driven gear back to the driver's direction without changing the overall ratio
why: The idler's tooth count cancels out of the ratio; it only changes direction or fills a gap.

prompt: Why is the efficiency of a real machine always less than 100%?
options: Some input work is lost to friction, and to lifting moving parts such as pulley blocks
Because the velocity ratio is always less than 1
Because energy is created in the machine
Because the load is always heavier than the effort
why: Losses mean output work is less than input work, so MA is less than VR.

prompt: When a small gear drives a larger gear, the output shaft has
options: lower speed and higher torque than the input
why: Ignoring losses, power = torque × speed is constant, so reducing speed increases torque.

prompt: The velocity ratio of a machine is
options: the distance moved by the effort divided by the distance moved by the load
the load divided by the effort
the output power divided by the input power
the effort divided by the load
why: VR depends only on geometry; MA = load/effort includes friction.

prompt: Work hardening (cold working) a copper sheet
options: decreases its hardness and increases its ductility
increases its hardness and strength but reduces its ductility
makes it a better electrical insulator
has no effect on its properties
why: Cold working multiplies and tangles dislocations, so further slip is harder.

prompt: A cold-worked brass part has become too hard to form further. Which treatment restores its ductility?
options: Quenching in water from room temperature
Annealing: heating above the recrystallisation temperature and cooling slowly
why: Annealing allows new strain-free grains to form (recrystallisation), softening the metal.

prompt: Hot working a metal (forming above its recrystallisation temperature) is used for large reductions because
options: the metal recrystallises as it is deformed, so it does not work harden and needs less force
it makes the metal harder than cold working
it gives a bright, accurate surface finish
why: Hot working needs less force and allows big shape changes, but gives scale and poorer tolerances than cold working.

prompt: Thermosoftening (thermoplastic) polymers can be remelted because their chains are
options: linear or branched and held together only by weak intermolecular forces
why: Heating overcomes the weak forces so chains slide; cooling sets them again.

prompt: Which polymer is a thermoset?
why: Epoxy cures by forming a cross-linked network that cannot be remelted.

prompt: An elastomer such as rubber can stretch a lot and spring back because it has
options: coiled chains with a small number of cross-links
why: Light cross-linking lets coiled chains straighten under load but pulls them back when released.

prompt: Which forming process is best for making a hollow PET drink bottle?
why: A heated preform is inflated inside a mould to make hollow containers.

prompt: Long lengths of constant cross-section, such as PVC pipe or aluminium window frame sections, are made by
why: Material is forced through a shaped die to give a continuous profile.

prompt: Which process heats a thermoplastic sheet and draws it over a mould to make shapes such as packaging trays?
why: Atmospheric pressure pushes the softened sheet onto the mould when air is removed.

prompt: Brass and bronze are both copper alloys. Brass contains copper and
why: Brass is Cu-Zn; bronze is Cu-Sn (tin).

prompt: Stainless steel resists rusting mainly because it contains at least about 10.5%
options: chromium, which forms a thin protective oxide layer
zinc, which acts as a sacrificial coating
why: Chromium forms a self-healing passive chromium oxide film.

prompt: Die casting is commonly used for zinc and aluminium appliance parts because it
options: produces parts with no porosity at all
produces large numbers of accurate, thin-walled parts with a good surface finish
is suitable for steel parts only
why: Molten metal is forced into a reusable steel die under pressure, which suits mass production.

prompt: Forging a spanner rather than machining it from solid bar improves toughness because forging
options: removes all carbon from the steel
makes the grain flow follow the shape of the part
why: Grain flow lines that follow the profile resist crack growth.

prompt: Fillers such as glass fibre or talc are added to polypropylene to
why: Fillers and reinforcements change mechanical properties and reduce the amount of polymer needed.

prompt: Plasticisers are added to PVC to
options: make it flexible, for example for cable insulation and hoses
why: Plasticisers sit between chains and let them move more easily.

prompt: Why are UV stabilisers added to polymers used outdoors?
options: To slow down degradation and embrittlement caused by sunlight
why: Ultraviolet light breaks polymer chains; stabilisers absorb or neutralise this.

prompt: Which statement about sand casting is correct?
options: It can only make flat parts
It suits large or complex metal parts in small numbers, but gives a rough surface finish
It is used to form thermoplastics
It produces the best surface finish of any process
why: Sand moulds are cheap and flexible but are destroyed each time and leave a rough surface.

prompt: Deep drawing is a process in which
options: metal powder is pressed and sintered
a hot billet is hammered between dies
sheet metal is pressed by a punch into a die to form a seamless hollow shape such as a sink or can
molten metal is poured into a sand mould
why: Deep drawing stretches sheet into cups and shells.

prompt: Which pair correctly matches a polymer with a typical appliance use?
options: ABS: tough, glossy housings for vacuum cleaners and toasters
why: ABS is tough, easily moulded and has a good surface finish for housings.

prompt: Injection moulding a thermoplastic involves
options: drawing a wire through a die
pressing a sheet over a mould with vacuum
heating granules and forcing the melt into a closed mould, where it cools and is ejected
why: Screw-fed melt is injected under pressure into a cooled mould cavity.

prompt: On a sectional view to AS1100, the cut surfaces are shown by
why: Hatching with thin lines at 45° shows material cut by the cutting plane.

prompt: According to AS1100, which part is normally NOT sectioned even when the cutting plane passes along it?
options: A shaft, bolt or rib cut lengthwise
why: Shafts, fasteners, ribs, webs and spokes are left unhatched when cut lengthwise so the view is clearer.

prompt: A cutting plane on an orthogonal drawing is shown by
options: a thin chain line, thick at the ends and at changes of direction, with arrows showing the viewing direction
why: The thickened ends and arrows plus letters (e.g. A-A) identify the section.

prompt: A half section is most suitable for
options: a flat plate with no holes
an asymmetrical part with no internal detail
a symmetrical part, showing the inside on one half and the outside on the other
why: Half sections show both exterior and interior of symmetrical parts in one view.

prompt: On an AS1100 drawing, linear dimensions are given in
why: Millimetres are assumed unless noted otherwise.

prompt: Which symbol is placed before a dimension to show the diameter of a circle?
why: Ø means diameter; R means radius; SR means spherical radius.

prompt: Projection (extension) lines in dimensioning should
options: touch the outline and stop at the dimension line
start with a small gap from the outline and extend a little past the dimension line
why: The gap keeps the outline clear; the slight overrun makes the dimension easy to read.

prompt: Why should dimensions not be given to hidden lines?
options: Hidden lines are less clear and can be misread; features should be dimensioned where they are seen as visible outlines
AS1100 forbids dashed lines on drawings
It doubles the number of dimensions
why: Dimensioning visible features in the view that shows their true shape avoids errors.

prompt: Parallel (datum) dimensioning is preferred over chain dimensioning when accuracy matters because
options: it does not need a datum
it allows any feature to be dimensioned twice
each dimension is taken from one datum, so tolerances do not accumulate
why: In a chain, small errors in each link add up; datum dimensioning avoids this build-up.

prompt: In unidirectional dimensioning, dimension figures are
options: written along each dimension line, read from the bottom or the right
all written to be read from the bottom of the sheet
placed inside the outline of the part
why: Unidirectional text is all horizontal; aligned text follows the dimension line.

prompt: The title block of an engineering drawing should include
options: the drawing title, scale, projection symbol, drawn by, date and drawing number
why: Title blocks carry the information needed to identify and interpret the drawing.

prompt: A drawing shows a dimension of 40 ± 0.05. This means the actual size must be
why: The tolerance gives the allowable variation either side of the nominal size.

prompt: Which line type shows the boundary of a partial or broken-out section?
options: A thin continuous freehand or zigzag line
why: A thin irregular line shows where material has been broken away.

prompt: An assembly drawing differs from a detail drawing because it
options: shows how parts fit together, with item numbers and a parts list, rather than full manufacturing dimensions for each part
shows every dimension of every part
why: Detail drawings define single parts for manufacture; assembly drawings show relationships between parts.

prompt: A bar has an overall length of 122 mm. Chain dimensions along it read 30, 50, 18 and one missing dimension at the end. What is the missing dimension?
why: The chain must add to the overall length: 122 − (30 + 50 + 18) = 24 mm.

prompt: A bar has an overall length of 126 mm. Chain dimensions along it read 35, 45, 22 and one missing dimension at the end. What is the missing dimension?
why: The chain must add to the overall length: 126 − (35 + 45 + 22) = 24 mm.

prompt: A bar has an overall length of 135 mm. Chain dimensions along it read 35, 55, 15 and one missing dimension at the end. What is the missing dimension?
why: The chain must add to the overall length: 135 − (35 + 55 + 15) = 30 mm.

prompt: A shaft is dimensioned Ø50 ± 0.2. What are its upper and lower limits of size?
why: Limits = nominal ± tolerance: 50 + 0.2 and 50 − 0.2.

prompt: A shaft is dimensioned Ø65 ± 0.05. What are its upper and lower limits of size?
why: Limits = nominal ± tolerance: 65 + 0.05 and 65 − 0.05.

prompt: A shaft is dimensioned Ø50 ± 0.05. What are its upper and lower limits of size?
why: Limits = nominal ± tolerance: 50 + 0.05 and 50 − 0.05.

prompt: The earliest wagon and early motor car brakes were mostly
options: simple block brakes: a wooden or leather-faced block levered against the wheel rim or tyre
why: A lever pressed a friction block on the wheel; these wore quickly and were weak in wet conditions.

prompt: Drum brakes became common on early cars because they
options: enclosed the friction surfaces, protecting them from dirt and water, and used expanding shoes on the inside of a drum
cooled better than any other design
were completely immune to brake fade
why: Internal expanding shoes are protected inside the drum and the design is self-energising.

prompt: Hydraulic brakes, introduced on cars in the early 20th century, were a major improvement over cable or rod brakes because they
options: transmit equal pressure to every wheel cylinder and multiply the pedal force
stop the engine instead of the wheels
why: By Pascal's principle pressure is the same throughout the fluid, giving balanced braking.

prompt: Disc brakes became widespread after success in motor racing in the 1950s mainly because they
options: are cheaper to make than drum brakes
dissipate heat better and resist brake fade under repeated hard stops
why: The exposed rotating disc sheds heat to the air quickly.

prompt: Air brakes, first developed by George Westinghouse for trains, are used on heavy trucks today because
options: compressed air can supply large braking forces and the system is fail-safe: loss of air pressure applies the brakes
air is a better lubricant than brake fluid
they are lighter than any hydraulic system
why: Spring brakes are held off by air pressure, so a leak applies them automatically.

prompt: Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) were introduced on production cars in the late 1970s. They rely on
options: wheel speed sensors and an electronic control unit that rapidly modulates brake pressure
a mechanical lever that locks the wheels
a parachute deployed from the car
why: The ECU detects a wheel about to lock and releases and reapplies pressure many times per second.

prompt: Asbestos was widely used in brake linings until it was banned in Australia in 2003 because
options: brake dust containing asbestos fibres causes serious lung diseases such as asbestosis and mesothelioma
it caused brake discs to rust
why: Asbestos withstood heat well but its fibres are carcinogenic, endangering mechanics and the public.

prompt: Regenerative braking in electric and hybrid vehicles improves efficiency because
options: it turns kinetic energy into heat faster
it removes the need for any friction brakes
it uses compressed air to slow the car
the motor acts as a generator, converting kinetic energy into electrical energy stored in the battery
why: Instead of wasting kinetic energy as heat, some is recovered to extend driving range.

prompt: Which is an environmental effect of conventional friction brakes?
options: They emit carbon dioxide directly from the pads
Brake wear releases fine particles, including metals, into the air and stormwater
why: Brake dust is a significant source of non-exhaust particulate pollution.

prompt: The introduction of ABS and electronic stability control most changed society by
options: increasing the top speed of cars
removing the need for driver licences
reducing the number and severity of crashes caused by skidding
why: Steering control is kept during emergency braking, preventing many loss-of-control crashes.

prompt: Engine (compression) brakes on trucks are restricted in some suburban areas because
options: they cause the engine to stop
why: Releasing compressed air from the cylinders makes a loud exhaust noise.

prompt: Copper has been reduced in modern brake pad formulations because
options: copper in brake dust washes into waterways and is toxic to aquatic life
why: Regulations in some places limit copper content to protect rivers and fish.

prompt: Dual-circuit hydraulic braking (two separate circuits) was introduced to improve safety because
options: if one circuit leaks, the other still provides braking to two wheels
it removes the need for a master cylinder
why: A single leak would otherwise cause total brake failure.

prompt: A power brake booster (servo) helps the driver by
options: using engine vacuum or a pump to add to the pedal force on the master cylinder
why: The booster multiplies pedal effort so lighter pedal forces give strong braking.

prompt: Which statement about the move from drum brakes to disc brakes is correct?
options: Discs were used before drums on early cars
Drums have completely disappeared from all vehicles
Drum brakes cool better than discs
Discs are self-cleaning and cool better, but drums are still often used at the rear of light vehicles because they are cheaper and suit a handbrake
why: Many small cars still use rear drums for cost and parking brake simplicity.

prompt: Brake fluid is hygroscopic. This creates a safety issue because absorbed water
options: lowers the boiling point, so vapour bubbles can form under heavy braking and the pedal goes soft
increases the friction of the pads
freezes the master cylinder in summer
makes the fluid more viscous so brakes lock
why: Vapour is compressible, so the pedal travels without applying pressure (vapour lock).

prompt: Bicycle brakes changed from rim brakes to disc brakes on many modern bikes mainly because disc brakes
options: are lighter than any rim brake
work more consistently in wet and muddy conditions and do not wear the rim
why: The rotor is away from road spray and rim wear no longer weakens the wheel.

prompt: Electronic brakeforce distribution (EBD) improves on basic ABS by
options: switching off the rear brakes permanently
automatically varying the braking force between front and rear wheels according to load and conditions
removing the need for brake pads
doubling the brake fluid pressure at all wheels
why: Optimal front/rear balance shortens stops without rear wheel lock-up.

prompt: Autonomous emergency braking (AEB) uses
options: radar, lidar or cameras to detect an imminent collision and apply the brakes automatically
why: Sensors and software can react faster than the driver to avoid or reduce a crash.

prompt: Train brakes on a long freight train must be fail-safe. Which design achieves this?
options: Brakes held off by air pressure in the brake pipe, so a broken pipe or uncoupling applies them on every wagon
Brakes that need electrical power to apply
Brakes applied only by the locomotive
Brakes applied by a cable from the driver
why: Loss of pressure, for any reason, results in braking rather than runaway.

prompt: A 15 kg brake test block on a level bench needs a horizontal force of 66.2 N to just start sliding. Find the coefficient of static friction (g = 9.8 m/s²).
A 25 kg brake test block on a level bench needs a horizontal force of 61.3 N to just start sliding. Find the coefficient of static friction (g = 9.8 m/s²).

why: Friction on two faces = 2μN = 3.20 kN; torque = 3.20 kN × 0.13 m = 416 N m.

prompt: A brake calliper clamps a disc with a force of 12 kN on each side (two pads). The pad friction coefficient is 0.45 and the pads act at an effective radius of 0.13 m. Find the braking torque on the disc.
why: Friction on two faces = 2μN = 10.8 kN; torque = 10.8 kN × 0.13 m = 1400 N m.

prompt: A brake calliper clamps a disc with a force of 8 kN on each side (two pads). The pad friction coefficient is 0.4 and the pads act at an effective radius of 0.12 m. Find the braking torque on the disc.
why: Friction on two faces = 2μN = 6.40 kN; torque = 6.40 kN × 0.12 m = 768 N m.

prompt: A 2200 kg car travelling at 40 km/h brakes to rest. How much kinetic energy must the brakes convert to heat?
why: v = 40/3.6 = 11.1 m/s; KE = ½mv² = 136 kJ. Speed must be in m/s.

prompt: A 900 kg car travelling at 110 km/h brakes to rest. How much kinetic energy must the brakes convert to heat?
why: v = 110/3.6 = 30.6 m/s; KE = ½mv² = 420 kJ. Speed must be in m/s.

prompt: A 1500 kg car travelling at 60 km/h brakes to rest. How much kinetic energy must the brakes convert to heat?
why: v = 60/3.6 = 16.7 m/s; KE = ½mv² = 208 kJ. Speed must be in m/s.

prompt: A 1000 kg ute moving at 20 m/s skids to a stop over 36 m. Using work = change in kinetic energy, find the average friction force.
A 2000 kg ute moving at 22 m/s skids to a stop over 30 m. Using work = change in kinetic energy, find the average friction force.
The brakes of a 1700 kg car bring it from 25 m/s to rest in 3 s. Find the average power dissipated by the brakes.
why: P = energy/time = ½mv²/t = 177 kW.

prompt: The brakes of a 1100 kg car bring it from 30 m/s to rest in 4 s. Find the average power dissipated by the brakes.
why: P = energy/time = ½mv²/t = 124 kW.

prompt: A master cylinder piston of diameter 20 mm is pushed with 1500 N. The calliper piston has a diameter of 57 mm. Find the force on the calliper piston.
why: Pressure is equal throughout (Pascal): F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁ = F₁ × (d₂/d₁)² = 12 200 N. Using the diameter ratio without squaring is a common error.

prompt: A master cylinder piston of diameter 20 mm is pushed with 1000 N. The calliper piston has a diameter of 54 mm. Find the force on the calliper piston.
why: Pressure is equal throughout (Pascal): F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁ = F₁ × (d₂/d₁)² = 7290 N. Using the diameter ratio without squaring is a common error.

prompt: A master cylinder piston of diameter 16 mm is pushed with 1000 N. The calliper piston has a diameter of 54 mm. Find the force on the calliper piston.
why: Pressure is equal throughout (Pascal): F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁ = F₁ × (d₂/d₁)² = 11 400 N. Using the diameter ratio without squaring is a common error.

prompt: A force of 1200 N acts on a master cylinder piston of diameter 25 mm. Find the hydraulic pressure produced.
why: A = πd²/4 = 491 mm²; p = F/A = 2.44 N/mm² = 2.44 MPa.
